summary_html: CPS **accepts** a report for **investigation/assessment**. CAPTA sets the floor for investigation procedures; CFSR evaluates timeliness, safety, and decision quality.
authority_html:
- **CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116)** — investigation standards tied to funding  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — timeliness & response conformity indicators

primary_citations.citation_text: Virginia - Va. Code Title 63.2, Chapter 15 (Child Abuse and Neglect – includes § 63.2-1509 reporting)
Virginia - Va. Code § 16.1-241(A) et seq. (Juvenile & Domestic Relations jurisdiction for abuse/neglect)

regulations_applicable.title: 22VAC40-705 - Child Protective Services (Virginia Administrative Code, Title 22, Agency 40)
22VAC40-201 - Permanency Services: Prevention, Foster Care, Adoption and Independent Living

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: The Court of Appeals of Virginia affirmed dismissal of a founded sexual abuse complaint, holding that the local department's failure to tape record the child victim's interview, absent any specific determination that recording was impractical or inappropriate under 22 VAC 40-705-80(B)(1), violated required procedure and was not harmless error.
key_cases.relevance: This is the controlling Virginia authority on the mandatory interview and recording procedures a CPS investigation must follow.
key_cases.quote: It was essential, therefore, for the hearing officer to have access to the precise substance of S.J.’s statements.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Fourth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the county, holding that a social worker's consented-to investigative home visit accompanied by deputies did not violate the Fourth Amendment because such visits are not measured by criminal search standards and consent to the caseworker's entry extended to the accompanying officials.
key_cases.relevance: This is the controlling Fourth Circuit rule on caseworker home entry and consent during a child protective investigation.
key_cases.quote: Furthermore, investigative home visits by social workers are not subject to the same scrutiny as searches in the criminal context.

key_cases.holding: The Court of Appeals of Virginia affirmed a founded sexual abuse disposition, holding that neither the statute nor due process requires the investigator to contact the accused before entering the initial determination, because the statutory amendment request, local conference and Commissioner's hearing supply the process due.
key_cases.relevance: It is the controlling Virginia holding that pre-determination contact with the accused is preferred but not legally required to validate an investigation.
key_cases.quote: While it is clearly preferable for an investigating official to contact the accused and any interested party, it is not a prerequisite to a valid determination.

key_cases.holding: The Court of Appeals of Virginia reversed, upholding the Department's child protective services guidelines and holding that a 'founded' disposition that only threatens reputation and speculative future consequences does not deprive the alleged abuser of a liberty or property interest requiring additional procedural safeguards.
key_cases.relevance: It holds the Department's function to be adjudicative as well as investigative, which is why the due process inquiry applies at all.
key_cases.quote: However, a person’s reputation alone is not a liberty or property interest and thus is not entitled to due process protection.

key_cases.case_name: Vosburg v. Department Of Social Services
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Fourth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for Virginia social workers, holding that they are absolutely immune from § 1983 liability arising from their decision to file a removal petition because that function is prosecutorial, while expressly declining to extend that immunity to their conduct in investigating whether a petition should be filed.
key_cases.relevance: The Court expressly refused to immunize the investigation that precedes a removal petition, which is why the investigative stage remains the litigable part of a Virginia CPS case.
key_cases.quote: We emphasize, however, that our grant of absolute immunity applies only to those activities of social workers that could be deemed prosecutorial.

timeline_requirements.deadline: No clock set by rule - initial safety assessment of the child's circumstances and threat of danger or harm, and a safety plan where appropriate, in both family assessments and investigations; the first face-to-face contact with the child is due within the response time set at intake, or within 24 hours when the victim child is younger than two (22VAC40-705-80(A)(1), (B)(1))
timeline_requirements.starts_from: The worker's first contact in the family assessment or investigation

timeline_requirements.deadline: 45 days (extendable to a total of 60 days on written justification, or to 90 days in a joint law-enforcement investigation)
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Statute sets no penalty; any extension requires written justification and the local department must notify the alleged abuser or neglector and the child's parents (Va. Code § 63.2-1505(B)(5); 22VAC40-705-120)
